speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER  THREATENED STRIKE OF PILOTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Transport. Did he receive notice from the St. Lawrence pilots to the effect that they would call a special general meeting at 12 o'clock tonight, unless the Minister of Transport finds an answer to the problems they brought before him last February?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER  THREATENED STRIKE OF PILOTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member for Charlevoix had sent me notice of the same question, I prepared an answer that might seem somewhat detailed, but I feel that it covers the present situation.
As the house knows, the Minister of Transport has the authority over pilotage in the four pilotage districts: the first one goes from Les Escoumins to Quebec city; the second one, from Quebec city to Montreal; the third one is Montreal harbour itself; and the fourth one goes from Montreal to Cornwall. From Cornwall to Kingston, Canadian pilots come under the Canada-United States great lakes program but they are members of the St. Lawrence pilots' federation or union none the less. A telegram I received late yesterday afternoon informed me that the pilots intend to walk off their jobs this evening probably in order to get certain financial and other advantages.
The dispute concerns the following points: the pilots of those districts work approximately nine months a year. The income from pilotage dues are divided equally among the pilots. Last year, the individual gross income of the pilots in the Les Escoumins-Quebec city district was a little over $16,300. After deduction of a rather large amount for expenses, their net income amounted to $14,700. That result is arrived at by dividing the total income by the number of pilots, after having made the proper deduction in that number to take into account absenteeism or sick leave for a period of more than ten working days. The working day over that period is established on the basis of the total number of days in the shipping season divided
Inquiries of the Ministry by the total number of pilotage hours during the season. It comes out to 4.7 hours per day.
In the Quebec-Montreal district, the gross income is slightly over $14,200 and the net income, after proper deduction for expenses, is just over $12,600 per pilot, for an average working day of 4.9 hours.
In the Montreal harbour district, the gross individual income is just over $12,200 and the net individual income amounts to just over $11,000 for an average working day of 3.1 hours.
In the Cornwall district, the gross individual income is a little over $13,000 and the net income is slightly over $12,300, the average working day being 5.3 hours.
The pilots in the Cornwall-Kingston district of the St. Lawrence river, while they are members of the same federation, come under the Canada-United States great lakes agreement. Any tariff agreement in that district is subject to the joint agreement signed with the United States. The gross income of the pilots in that group, during the last year, amounted to $15,900 and the net income to $14,900, after deducting expenses.
The principal requests made by the pilots for the present season are as follows:
With regard to the Cornwall district, an increase in full trip fees charged to the vessels, which would mean an increase of approximately 20 per cent in the pilots' income. At the Montreal harbour, an increase in fees or a transfer of certain duties from the river pilots to the harbour pilots, which would increase their income from 6 to 10 per cent. For the river group at Montreal, an increase in the number of pilots as well as a 15 per cent increase in income, which would make it necessary to increase the tariff by approximately 18 per cent. The Quebec district has not formulated any important request with regard to the tariff structure; its petition deals with questions of secondary importance.
The pilots have also indicated that they disagree on the method adopted by the department to establish the average gross revenue with regard to the number of pilots actually employed during a year, in order to calculate the average income, and they asked the department to set the average according to a method which, when the calculation is made, will show that the pilots' yearly income is lower than the above-mentioned figures.

Inquiries of the Ministry
In fact, the pilots are in a special position and their income is derived from the shipowners who, in most cases, are obliged to pay pilotage fees whether they use a pilot or not. The shipowners most interested in the matter, that is the Shipping Federation of Canada, the Dominion Marine Association and the Canadian Shipowners Association, have strongly intimated that, in their opinion, increases in pilotage fees are not justified this year.
The Shipping Federation, the main user, indicated its willingness to study with the pilots, starting with the Montreal harbour group, a new approach to the yearly problem of the pilots' income. Therefore, I wrote today to the pilots and the shipowners to propose in that respect direct talks between the two sides with a view to ascertaining whether an agreement and a new solution to the problem can be reached.
Some other less important questions are still under study by my department and we expect to submit other proposals in due course. Thus we had already agreed-and had so informed the pilots-to license a small number of new pilots in the river district at Montreal.
I want to point out further that the river about Montreal is not yet open to navigation, so soon after winter, and that the movement of ships below Montreal is still light.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall I report the resolution?

Mr. Chairman, I am obliged at this time to register a protest. I have no intentions of opposing the proposal now before us. However, I believe it is timely that we recall to our minds the very origin of parliament itself, something which goes back approximately 1,000 years in the history of our democratic civilization. I believe that political democracy as we know it is being whittled away by the procedure of which this House of Commons is now being asked to approve.
I agree that incidents of this kind have happened in the past. However, the mere fact that I committed a sin some 20 years ago does not give me any licence to commit a similar sin at this time. It has always been the right of parliament to withhold funds that have been requested until parliament has been satisfied not only as to the proposed expenditure of the funds but also as to the method by which the government expects to collect the funds.
This government is asking for interim supply prior to the introduction of a budget. I feel that this is a violation of our tradition, even though I am willing to admit that such violations have happened in the past. The latest research information that I have been able to obtain is to the effect that it happened last in the year 1946.
I know that the government is able to carry on at any time under warrants issued by the governor in council. I regret very much that I did not adequately voice my opinion the last time the Financial Administration Act was amended. I believe this parliament committed a basic error at the time the last amendment was made to that Act. The government now asks for interim supply, but we members of parliament have no knowledge of how the revenues are to be collected. I feel that the introduction of a budget is basic and ought to precede any request for interim

supply. We have the age old cry, "No taxation without representation". We are now asked in effect to vote money that really does not exist as parliament has not yet been asked to vote the method of collecting revenues for the current fiscal year.
I feel it is a gross breach of parliamentary tradition for us to be asked to agree to vote interim supply before we have been told how the government proposes to collect the money. I know the government can well raise the argument that there are existing taxation laws but in my opinion this is an argument that does not hold water. If it is valid for parliament to be asked annually for the approval of expenditures, it is equally valid for parliament to have the right to ask the government annually as to the manner in which it proposes to collect the revenue. I believe it has almost always been the case in Canadian parliamentary history that the government of the day has informed parliament as to how it intended to collect the revenue before asking for approval of methods of distributing that revenue. Interim supply may have been granted before the introduction of a budget, but that is no excuse for continuing this evil. We have voted interim supply after the adoption of a budget, but this is an entirely different matter. After the government has announced its intentions with respect to how it proposes to collect the money it is completely legitimate, in my opinion, for that government to ask for interim supply, but in this particular case the government has not brought forward a budget. It has not even made any announcement that we will have a budget before an election is called. We have yet to receive an assurance from the minister or the government that there is going to be a budget. Anybody can make promises, Mr. Chairman. It is very easy to make promises in an irresponsible manner. I am beginning to doubt whether there is any intention on the part of the government to introduce a budget before there is an appeal to the people.
I never expected to see happen what took place in 1958, when the government for pure political expediency resorted in an unprecedented way to the abuse of governor general's warrants in order to carry on the business of the country. We now have to face the situation that the government is asking for interim supply before giving the house any indication of how it intends to collect the necessary revenue. In my view this is unethical and unworthy of our traditions.
However, as I indicated when I began my remarks, this is a bread and butter issue. The pay cheques of thousands of people depend

upon the granting of interim supply, and I do not find it in my heart to vote against the interim supply now requested by the government.

On clause 3-Application of part I.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
Before clause 3 carries I have a comment to make. This relates to a question I asked the minister yesterday about the compilation of figures by the dominion bureau of statistics. The minister replied as follows, as reported in Hansard at page 2501:
-I can refer the committee to the recent report on the Canadian balance of international payments in 1960 and the international investment position, page 62, where the bureau itself has fully set out a summary of the methods it follows in compiling these statistics and makes an assessment of their accuracy and reliability.
I obtained a copy of the particular document to which the minister referred, dominion bureau of statistics publication catalogue No. 67-201, and looked at page 62. I read the information given by the dominion

Corporations and Labour Unions bureau of statistics to indicate how they arrived at these particular figures, and I found this very interesting and enlightening statement:
Briefly, while the principal source of the bureau's estimates of the foreign investment position is the capital structure reflected on consolidated balance sheets of enterprises classified according to the principal activity pursued, the source utilized most extensively for estimating the comparable aggregate capital value of selected Canadian industries is the summation of unconsolidated balance sheets of fully tabulated companies found in taxation statistics, as compiled by the Department of National Revenue, classified according to activity of the individual company.
The dominion bureau of statistics, therefore say they compile their statistics in this booklet to which we have referred about foreign control and foreign investment from the statistics published by the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue. I assume that General Motors, to which the minister referred yesterday, is a private corporation and pays income taxes, although it may not pay as much as it should. Canadian General Electric was another company to which the minister referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
Canadian General Electric
is a public company. I did refer to it, but it is a public company.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
In any event the minister did refer to General Motors, and so did other hon. gentlemen, as being a private company. I assume that General Motors and other private companies in Canada file information with the Department of National Revenue as required by the Income Tax Act. This information, then, is used by the dominion bureau of statistics after it has been processed by the Department of National Revenue, and the bureau of statistics compile the statistics which they give us in this particular document.
May I make another reference to something in these statistics at page 58 of the same publication to which I referred, the Canadian balance of international payments in 1960 and international investment position. This is under the section dealing with foreign ownership and control of Canadian industries, in the right hand column, and reads as follows:
Perhaps the most striking feature of these series, viewed in the perspective of a third of a century,-
Remember, this is over a third of a century, 30 to 34 years, about which they are talking now.
-viewed in the perspective of a third of a century, embracing depression and boom, war and peace, is the consistency of the direction of the changes. Foreign ownership of Canadian manufacturing has inched up from 38 per cent in 1926 to 51 per cent in 1959,-

I do not know that "inched up" is the appropriate term; perhaps "leaped up" would be more correct.
-and control has gone from 35 per cent to 57 per cent. Foreign ownership of mining and smelting has also reflected an almost uninterrupted growth from 37 per cent in 1926 to 59 per cent in 1959, and control has risen from 38 per cent to 61 per cent.
This document then deals with other sections of industry in the same way, using statistics which have already been placed on the record. The point is that so far as the bureau of statistics are concerned, they have been compiling this information since 1926 and are still compiling it. They are compiling it from the Department of National Revenue statistics, and as I said I assume that all companies, private and public, make returns as required by the Income Tax Act.
What has the government done about this information which it already has, and has had for the past five years? What has it done about the growth from 57 per cent to 59 per cent, an increase of two percentage points, in the foreign control of Canadian industries? Since this government took office in 1957 it has talked about the development of national unity, about our national heritage being repatriated, about developing Canadian ownership, Canadian control, Canadian distribution, and so on.
All it has done in that five year period has been to draft Bill No. C-70 last year and Bill No. C-38 this year, place them before parliament and say "Now we want to compile another bunch of statistics; the ones we have are no good." This will mean that in future years the dominion bureau of statistics will be able to bring out another publication and the government will then be in the position of again doing nothing about them. A bill of this nature is just a sham and a farce in relation to what we already know, and taking into account what could have been done about these matters.
On page 60 of its publication the dominion bureau of statistics points out that the rubber industry was 98 per cent foreign controlled in 1959, an increase in such control over the last two years. It also points out that the automobile and parts industry was 97 per cent foreign controlled, an increase of 2 per cent over 1957. It also states that the electrical apparatus section of manufacturing is 81 per cent under foreign control, an increase of 4 per cent over the last two years. The chemicals industry is 77 per cent foreign controlled, and other manufacturing is 61 per cent foreign controlled. It is the same all the way down the line, with the agricultural machinery industry being 55 per cent foreign controlled as compared with 38 per cent just two years ago.

This is information which the government already has at its fingertips. It is information compiled by the very same people whom the government will be asking to compile the same statistics under the provisions of Bill No. C-38. If it is not duplication, then what additional information does the government want? It seems to me that the government is speaking with its tongue in its cheek and is not being fully truthful and honest with parliament and the public about its desire to develop a national identity, national understanding and control of our industries.
The government has had these statistics ever since it came into office. These statistics have been compiled and built up since 1926, but now the government wants to superimpose another set of statistics on what it already has in order to get information relating to corporations and the degree of foreign control exercised over them. Detailed information in regard to the extent of foreign control and domination over unions would perhaps be of some interest to somebody, but if that is what the government wants, then why does it not bring in a separate piece of legislation stipulating that unions have to report that information?
I make that suggestion, but at the same time I contend that a separate bill is not necessary, as the information is already accessible. The minister knows that the constitutions of unions have to be filed with the Department of Labour. At least that is the case in British Columbia, where unions are required to do so under the provisions of the labour relations act before they can gain any benefit-if one could call it that-from the labour code in British Columbia.
I have not carefully examined the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, but it seems to me that, if not under that act then under some other statute, every union must file its constitution and every collective agreement between union and management with the Department of Labour. I was told so by Professor Fred Carrothers of the University of British Columbia, who has done extensive work in the field of arbitration in labour disputes and the use of injunctions in those disputes. I take his word for it because, as I say, he has done research into this matter.
If the government wants specific information about unions it should bring in a separate bill dealing with them, but it is a well known fact that every union in Canada has a set of letters attached after its name which invariably give an indication of other groups to which each individual union is affiliated. Indeed the union to which I belong, the international woodworkers union has attached to its name "(A.F.I.-C.l.O.-C.L.C.)," which means 26207-1-161

It is a sham and a farce because it is a complete misrepresentation and distortion of what this bill will accomplish. It is a complete misinterpretation and distortion of the picture with regard to the availability of statistics, and it is a misrepresentation of the objectives that this bill seeks to accomplish.

The only hon. member who has just discovered that the information the dominion bureau of statistics was quoting comes from "Taxation Statistics" is the hon. member for Skeena. Everybody in the house has known for a good many years that the Department of National Revenue makes this information public, and has known that the dominion bureau of statistics has relied upon it for many years.
What the hon. member has sought to do is mislead this committee, and all those who may have the misfortune to read his speech, into believing that because the Department of National Revenue publishes a green book called "Taxation Statistics" somehow or other the dominion bureau of statistics has access to the details that are contained in income tax returns, and that the information in individual returns with respect to corporate activities, methods and payments are available to the bureau and the government at large.
It may be, indeed it is my hope, that the hon. gentleman is himself under that illusion, but I doubt it. The serious issue I take with him is, that unless he is under that illusion, he would have willingly misled the committee had his speech been allowed to stand unchallenged.
The dominion bureau of statistics does not see any individual income tax return. It does not know how General Motors of Canada, to name one company which has been named, carries on its operations. Nor does any member of the government possess any information on the basis of a tax return with the exception of the Minister of National Revenue, if he reads it; and even if he reads it he is not at liberty to tell the government about it. So no other member of the government knows what is contained in the return of General Motors or in the return of any other company which files a return.
And even if this information were available it would be nothing as compared with what we are asking for under this bill- information which includes such matters as charges for royalties and research and similar payments and charges for various services including engineering, architectural, legal, accounting and auditing services and so on, showing the fees and charges separately in


each case. And there is all the other information which clause 4 would require these corporations to file.
The suggestion inherent in the hon. member's speech a moment ago is that this kind of information is available to the dominion bureau of statistics. That suggestion is just unfounded and malevolent nonsense. It is because such information is not available anywhere that we have introduced this bill and made it necessary to report this and other information which, if it were not for this measure, would never come to the knowledge of the government, the dominion bureau of statistics or anyone else.
There is another thing that the hon. member carefully omitted to point out. The dominion bureau of statistics itself-and I gave the hon. member the page reference- clearly draws attention to the fact that information in the form in which it comes to them does not enable that organization to make speedy, accurate and 100 per cent reliable statistical summaries. Here is what they say on page 62:
In the post-war years the series has made extensive use of the condensed balance sheets published by the Department of National Revenue in the annual report on taxation statistics. As this material does not become available for a considerable period after the time to which it relates, the bureau's series involving Canadian as well as foreign investment cannot be produced as currently as statistics of international investment. The condensed balance sheet figures are not ideal for estimating the total value of selected Canadian industries comparable to the foreign investment record. Corporations are not permitted by the Department of National Revenue to file consolidated reports, while for obvious reasons consolidated balance sheets are used wherever possible in the records of international investment.
I gave the page reference of that quotation to the hon. member yesterday, but he carefully avoided drawing attention to the fact that the dominion bureau points out that it is not in a position to get accurate, up to date particulars of the kind so necessary not only if detailed knowledge is to be available but also if adequate statistical summaries are to be compiled and published.
So I could go on indicating the inadequacies, the glaring omissions, the misconstructions, the misinterpretations and the misleading effects of what the hon. member has been saying about this bill for the past three days. There is one thing I should like to suggest and that is with regard to the matter of the labour unions. I am prepared to discuss those provisions fully when we get to them, but I do hope, Mr. Chairman, that at this stage you will not permit a general discussion of the trade union position, which should be reserved until we come to that part of the bill dealing with trade unions. I make this observation now because on

several occasions the hon. member for Skeena began to get into this question of unions. In my opinion the discussion is sufficiently general now; indeed, it is over-general now that we are dealing with the clauses of the bill.
I suggest it would be a mistake to get into a general discussion at this time of the question of trade unions which, I suspect, the hon. member is trying to introduce.
As to the purpose of the bill, and the charges and allegations which have been made, I can only conclude by saying that such a deliberate obfuscation of the objects and intent of the bill, such a distortion of its effects, such misrepresentation as to what it does, can only give rise to the thought that the hon. member's speeches are made for political purposes. In any event, I certainly say that what is being done here now and what has been done for the past three days will, if continued, have the effect of depriving Canada of the benefits of an advantageous piece of legislation which would place the government for the first time in history in possession of full details as to how foreign owned corporations and subsidiaries in Canada carry on their affairs.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Perhaps I should make a few remarks in connection with this measure. By this bill the respective railways and undertakings of three wholly owned leased subsidiaries of Canadian Pacific, including all their respective powers, rights, privileges, franchises, assets, effects and properties will be vested in Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which company will assume all their liabilities, obligations and duties.
The names of the three subsidiary companies and their locations are as follows: Joliette and Brandon Railway Company, Quebec; The Saint John Bridge and Railway Extension Company, New Brunswick; and The Saint Stephen and Milltown Railway Company, New Brunswick.
The petition for the bill has been made jointly by Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the three subsidiary companies concerned, in accordance with resolutions passed by the directors and shareholders of all companies.
Joliette and Brandon Railway Company was incorporated by statutes of Quebec (1905)
5 Edward VII, chapter 56 and vested with the franchises, subventions, railway, property, privileges, easements and appurtenances of the Montreal and Lac Maskinonge Railway Company, incorporated by statutes of Quebec (1887) 50 Victoria, chapter 68; the said company was leased to Canadian Pacific Railway Company for 94 years from January 1, 1906, by an indenture of lease dated October 31, 1906.

The Saint John Bridge and Railway Extension Company was incorporated by statutes of New Brunswick (1881) 44 Victoria, chapter 44; the said company was leased to Canadian Pacific Railway Company for 999 years from December 31, 1943 by an indenture of lease dated October 31, 1943.
The Saint Stephen and Milltown Railway Company was incorporated by statutes of New Brunswick (1886) 49 Victoria, chapter 17; the said company was leased to Canadian Pacific Railway Company for 99 years from May 1, 1897 by an indenture of lease dated April 21, 1897.
All three companies are presently operated by Canadian Pacific Railway Company as part of its system under the provisions of the abovementioned long term leases. It is intended to continue to operate these companies as part of the Canadian Pacific system after the legislation comes into effect so long as economic conditions warrant their operation. The proposed legislation will not affect the public in any way.
The purpose of the bill is to effect a simplification in the corporate organization of Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It will eliminate unnecessary clerical work which is now required by reason of the existence of these subsidiary companies.
In 1958 a similar act was enacted by the parliament of Canada, vesting in Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the railways and undertakings of nine other wholly owned leased subsidiaries of Canadian Pacific Railway Company; the act in question is chapter 54 of the statutes of Canada 1958. Other similar acts vesting in Canadian Pacific Railway Company the railways and undertakings of wholly owned leased subsidiaries were enacted in the years 1955, 1956 and 1957. Altogether 35 wholly owned leased subsidiary companies have been vested to date in Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
The present bill is identical with chapter 54 of the statutes of Canada, 1958, and the other vesting acts, except that this year only three wholly owned subsidiaries of Canadian Pacific are to be vested and that no dissolution of these subsidiary companies is sought as the said three companies were incorporated by provincial legislation.
The practical effect of the ownership by Canadian Pacific of all the capital stock and bonds, where issued, of the three companies involved, combined with the leases of the companies to Canadian Pacific Railway Company is tantamount to the amalgamation of these companies with Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The act sought from the parliament of Canada will complete the matter.

A similar statement was made on other occasions. On the occasion just referred to I assumed something would be done. I was pleased with the results of negotiations that took place among hon. members of the

Exchequer Court
Liberal and New Democratic parties and the hon. members for Davenport and Marquette. There seemed to be agreement that something could be done without any particular fanfare and fuss. It is our sincere desire to have this problem solved. If it can be solved through negotiations, all the better.
We are now faced with the terrific rush of private hon. members to get their bills on the order paper which indicates that dissolution may be just around the corner, and the problem has not yet been solved.
We are concerned about recent rumours about negotiations that have taken place between parties in the house. Probably this is true. The hon. member for Skeena and I have shown an interest in this matter but with the exception of the discussions with the two hon. members referred to, little discussion has taken place that would indicate a solution is in sight.
Much publicity is being given to the other place and some of the hon. members of that chamber. More attention is being paid to their need for publicity than to the need of solving the problem.
Some may say the problem cannot be, need not be or should not be solved. Certainly the method of solution is open to debate and in making the suggestion I am today I feel I am offering a proposal capable of being implemented by the government without cost which may even result in putting a few dollars in the federal treasury.
On March 22 of this year Hon. Senator Pouliot raised some questions about this matter in relation to the British North America Act. The Minister of Justice should consider that many provinces operate divorce courts under licence of the federal government. Senator Pouliot has done considerable research in the field and is under the impression that only the Exchequer Court of Canada or another federal court could handle divorce cases because provincial courts or any other courts are ultra vires of the constitution. That may be a valid point. Those divorce courts already in existence may be in conflict with the British North America Act. I have contended that the present set-up is unconstitutional.
The easy way for the government to solve the problem would be to appoint two or three additional judges to the Exchequer Court of Canada and let them handle the divorce cases there with the existing facilities.
I know the Exchequer Court of Canada is not presently equipped to deal with these cases but they could be dealt with there expeditiously and economically. There is a higher appeal court over the Exchequer Court of Canada. I understand that the exchequer

court now handles mainly income tax, corporation tax and other appeal cases.
I do not wish to examine all the many suggestions that have been made for solving the problem, many of which are unrealistic. The suggestion has been made that all these cases should be dealt with by the other place. The attitude taken is: Let the senators be the divorce court for parliament. It would be perfectly all right if the government were to sit down with the members of the other parties and decide what type of rules they could provide for a court which would make, in my opinion, a complete change in the Senate operation. However, first I think we should like to know what the present government's intention is in relation to Senate reform. If we are going to reform the Senate radically, I think this reform would have some effect on the divorce court that could be established in that place. I believe that at the present time there is only one man who is well enough informed in this particular field to be able to operate that divorce court. If we are going to retire the present members of the Senate at the age of 80, then this gentleman will no longer be available for that job.
I also believe that we should be obliged to set up a proctor in order to protect the rights of this house. I think we should also be obliged to make it necessary to bring back to the House of Commons a report on what happened in the other place in relation to the detective agencies that appear before it, the lawyers who appear before it, the taxation schemes that are put into effect in each of these cases, and to bring back to parliament a report indicating the desires for reform that would take place from time to time as the operation of a court in the Senate developed. I think this would have to be done before there can be any agreement.
It may be said that this is not too important a matter. However, let me read a few excerpts from some editorials which have appeared in the press. In one which appeared in the Toronto daily Star of July 16, 1960, we find this statement:
Parliamentary divorces are the scandal of the nation. They have long cried out for reform. The government should set up the necessary preliminary study at once, possibly by a special committee of the house.
The terms of reference must go beyond a switch of Quebec and Newfoundland divorces from parliament to a court.
It then goes on to state what other things they should do. Another editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 5, 1962, in referring to discussions we have held in this House of Commons, contained this statement:

-illuminated the farcical nature of the divorce machinery by Insisting upon debating the merits of individual bills in the Commons, thus disrupting the parliamentary timetable.
Then it goes on to say this:
Parliament's first progressive move should be to hand the Newfoundland and Quebec petitions to a competent federal court. The second move, and one which should not be long delayed, should be the liberalization of the divorce laws.
Another editorial which appeared in the Star Weekly of August 5, 1961, had this to say:
-Parliament degrading its function by becoming a legislative Reno, the logical and easy move would be appointment of a royal commission to inquire into Canadian divorce procedures.
Then it goes on to say this:
But while parliament continues to seek so assiduously for revisions of present divorce procedure, it might logically recommend a commission. As yet, however, it has not chosen to do so.
It goes on further to state this:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of his remarks, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) mentioned that himself and his colleague from Skeena (Mr. Howard) devoted a great deal of time during the present parliament to the study of the question of divorce. We were certainly aware of that fact, because I feel that they have taken up a considerable amount of the time of the house.
In the dying days of the present parliament, I should like to point out, if I may, that the hon. member for Timiskaming and his colleague from Skeena seemed to me very much impressed and even obsessed by problems of procedure in this respect. I think that this matter of procedure is altogether a minor one and that we should concern ourselves with the problem arising from this bill, especially from the moral and legal points of view.
I am against this bill for two main reasons:
In the first place, I am against divorce. Second, I am opposed to the illegal bill introduced by the hon. member for Timiskaming.
I am against divorce because it is the worst social evil man has ever known, in spite of his social and intellectual achievements.
A short review of the history of the world shows that divorce, this release of one's obligations under both natural and family law, has been on the upsurge not in highly moral societies but in decadent, lascivious and worn out civilizations.
The history of Rome and of France are but two examples of this.
History does show that divorce was established in Rome not when the empire was going through its period of greatness, but when it was becoming decadent.
The divorce problem suddenly appeared in France at the time of the French revolution.
[Mr. Peters.}
Divorce creates disorder in the family. It destroys its basic element. Moreover, it defeats the objects of marriage, which are to bring children into the world and to raise them, to abate the lusts of the flesh and to provide for mutual help.
Finally, I am opposed to divorce because it kills what the Creator has instilled in us, the desire to be closer to Him and to maintain our human dignity during our whole life.
A study of the social evolution of countries where divorce has been permitted reveals that the individual who took this course headed towards his downfall and away from his human dignity. Statistics indicate that 80 per cent of the suicides involve divorced persons.
The more courts you set up to consider divorces, the more divorces you will have, and divorce cases will increase.
I think that in the Canadian context of Christian morality, one must make all possible efforts to make it more difficult to get a divorce. I do not accept the allegation made by the hon. member for Timiskaming who, at the outset of his remarks, called the attention of the house to the fact that if divorce cases were referred to the exchequer court, that would reduce the cost of obtaining divorces for Canadians.
We should leave things as they are. The fact that divorce is extremely costly is all to the good, because it will lessen this social evil which afflicts both families and individuals.
To set the record straight, I would say that the more divorce courts we have, the more divorce cases are heard, thus contributing to an increase in the number of divorces. Allow me to give you a few statistics concerning divorce throughout Canada.
In 1960, there were 38.6 divorces per 100,000 people in Canada; in British Columbia, the ratio was 100 divorces per 100,000 inhabitants. Meanwhile, the percentage in Quebec was only 9.4; in Ontario it was 46.9 and in Alberta, 74.5. Newfoundland sets the example with the lowest rate: 1.3 per cent.
These figures justify the stand taken by the two provinces which object to the establishment of divorce courts.
At present, divorce petitions in Canada are not a matter of right; it is a privilege, a favour, an exception. Consequently, if divorce

petitions do not constitute a right, they cannot be referred to a federal court. Of course, some provinces have established provincial divorce courts; that is their privilege.
I respect other people's opinions, but I ask that mine be respected also. To refer divorce cases to a federal court, namely the exchequer court is, in my opinion, to give that court authority over the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland, whereas it has no jurisdiction over those provinces at present in matters of divorce. Since petitions for divorce are not a right but an exception and a privilege, I claim that they cannot as such be referred to a federal court, whether it be the exchequer court or another court which hears petitions of right not cases of privilege.
The hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned in the course of his remarks that the country's constitution, the British North America Act, would not allow the establishment of divorce courts in the provinces.
He probably had in mind section 26 of the British North America Act, which deals with the legislative authority reserved to the parliament of Canada, marriage and divorce coming under section 26.
Using the same argument, I maintain that it is contrary to the British North America Act to propose to refer to the exchequer court the matter of divorce, a matter which is necessarily related, through its ramifications, connections and consequences, to the field of civil rights. As far as the solemnization of marriage is concerned, according to section 92, subsections 12 and 13, civil rights are involved which come exclusively under provincial jurisdiction.
Indeed, the province of Quebec, of which I am a representative in this house, objects to divorce, because it is an action which is not recognized in our civil law. Quebec's hard-won civil law, which was earned through the historic events of 1763 and the Treaty of Paris when freedom of worship was meant to be conceded, with certain restrictions of course, through the Quebec Act in 1774 and particularly through the different British North America Acts, finds recognition in subsection 13 of section 92.
That is precisely one of the basic reasons why Lower Canada, that is the province of Quebec, signed that federation agreement of 1867. It was in order to safeguard its civil rights.
Exchequer Court
Section 185 of the Civil Code of the province of Quebec reads as follows:
Marriage can only be dissolved by the natural death of one of the parties; while both live, it is indissoluble.
Because of those constitutional, legal, and historical reasons, I do not acknowledge the legality of transferring to the exchequer court a matter which would affect civil rights of the province of Quebec.
Of course, I am still considering the question. It is a very serious problem which must be considered at length. I am still wondering why, in 1867, in order to eliminate some anomalies (this is not the only one) marriage was not left under the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures?
There also exist some anomalies in the economic field, where the provinces and the federal government, due to the changes we have been experiencing in 1962, feel shackled.
We can see the lines of thought in Canada converging toward the repatriation of our constitution which will be amended with the consent of all parties concerned.
I hope this point of view we are submitting today will be duly considered.
In ending my remarks, as I want to allow other members to express their views, I declare that I do not recognize the legality of divorce.
In the province of Quebec, we do not want divorce courts, either provincial or federal.
We respect the wish of all other Canadians, and we think that those citizens who request this favour of an exceptional nature ask for a privilege which cannot be established as of right before the exchequer court.

Mr. Speaker, I extend to the mover of this bill my congratulations. This proposal to take from the Canadian House of Commons the detailed examination of so many of these cases which have been sent here in the past has my support. There have been a lot of anomalies in connection with our practice and procedure, such as the system whereby the other place is given certain jurisdiction to entertain some of these actions, with none of the safeguards which are found in our ordinary courts; the attempt to make our standing committee an appeal body without any examination of witnesses but merely through a perusal of the transcript of evidence and without having any specific standing orders

Exchequer Court
to govern us in our review. It seems to me that something should be changed, if possible.
I say this without subscribing to the views which I have heard expressed that it is a discredit to the parliament of Canada to be dealing with these matters. It is my firm opinion that we are the ultimate court of appeal and, as such, even the most humble of the citizens of this country should not be denied access to parliament if the occasion arises. I subscribe also to that view. I think the principle which the mover of this bill has in mind might well be a good one. I appreciate what the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) has in mind. He says he is opposed to divorce, and so am I. Unfortunately, sometimes circumstances do occur just as circumstances bring about the commission of a criminal offence, and they leave us with no alternative.
In considering what we can do, I should like first to express the hope that in this case the two provincial governments mentioned in the bill will take the first step of establishing domestic courts. These domestic courts should first direct their attention to trying to minimize this alarmingly high rate of divorce by exhausting all the methods of conciliation and compromise which are available. I have every reason to believe, and I say this from my own personal experience in the practice of my profession, that there are many things which could be done by provincial courts if they had complete responsibility for taking intermediate steps. However, this is probably irrelevant to the consideration of the bill.
I admire the courage of the mover of this particular bill. This is a matter which fairly bristles with difficulties, such as are bound to be involved in any matter that involves human relationships. These difficulties involve questions of jurisdiction and questions of a legal nature. For example, the bill which the hon. member has moved would purport to give jurisdiction to the exchequer court. As I pointed out when I spoke on this matter last year, the exchequer court today is a court composed of judges who, if they do not have the knowledge when they go to that court obtain it later, have knowledge of certain technical aspects of disputes covering patents, copyrights and matters of a financial nature. This proposal would involve the creation of a branch of the court and the appointment of a number of judges. When I spoke last year I mentioned that, as presently constituted, the exchequer court makes no provision for appeal. The right of appeal is limited to matters involving more than $500. If the amount involved is less than that, there must be, if my memory serves me correctly, leave obtained from a judge of the supreme court 
and the matter must include the study of certain technical aspects of the statutes of the provinces.
If we drove the petitioners for divorce into the exchequer court as the result of the enactment of this bill, these petitioners would be deprived of the right of appeal. Then, there is the question of alimony which arises in these issues. In all these matters, it is the innocent and unfortunate children who are often the victims. If this particular measure were enacted, the exchequer court would be charged with the responsibility of pronouncing the dissolution of the marriage, if the facts warranted it. The petitioners or respondents, whoever had the responsibility for the children, would then have to go to another court to settle the question of alimony and maintenance. This, Mr. Speaker, I believe is quite wrong. These people would be put to the expense and the difficulty of repeating the evidence because in both types of action precisely the same thing has to be proven. This, I could not accept.
I am going to limit my remarks by pointing out to the hon. member in whose name the bill stands that I have sympathy with the principle that has caused him to bring the bill forward, but I do not think it will serve the purposes which it is aimed to secure. After all, while we have an issue here which needs to be dealt with, we must examine closely the means by which the control we seek can be gained. I do not think these means are sufficient, but as I am sure there are other hon. members who wish to speak I shall not say anything more at this time. I have expressed my views and would like to hear what other hon. members may have to say.

speechtext:
I do not know whether or not the committee proposes to deal with the subparagraphs, but since no one else rises I propose to rise in respect of (J) of subparagraph (iii). There is a matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister who is piloting this bill through the house, namely, the matter of insurance. If, in fact, this committee is dealing with a bill, the purpose of which is to obtain information as it appears, then surely this is not just a matter of legislative peeping-tomism. Surely our purpose is to obtain information and, thereafter, if legislation is necessary to counteract anything, new legislation will be introduced. I would assume, from the opening speech made by the minister in introducing this bill to the committee, the purpose is to ensure that those who operate within Canada operate primarily for the

good of Canada. It would appear, then, that it is imperative that all members of the committee attempt to strengthen this bill and to obtain as much information as will be necessary to prove or disprove allegations which have been made in the past.
An allegation has been made to me, and I believe previously to the government in a brief submitted by the insurance company representatives in Canada, about the fact that there has been considerable financial blood letting of Canadian corporations which are foreign controlled by a peculiar device, in that where formerly these Canadian companies placed through local insurance agents or brokers insurance of various types such as life insurance, fire insurance and insurance on automobiles, not only on company fleets but on individual cars owned by individual employees, as a result of influence from United States head offices these policies have been withdrawn by gentle pressure from within the corporations. The employees in some cases have been influenced, and in other cases Canadian corporations have been influenced to place their insurance elsewhere.
In particular, without reference to the names of the corporations, which are Canadian corporations subsidiary to United States corporations, or to the insurance companies concerned, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that on at least two occasions this has happened in my own locality. Niagara Falls, as is generally known, is an industrial area and something like 2 per cent of the industries in the area are Canadian corporations. In the last few years, and I do not propose to say five years or four years or ten years, but in the last few years, this has happened. In one case, the local agents had written policies of fire insurance on local buildings and, in the process of a few months a pattern became obvious whereby the Canadian company began to cancel the insurance placed through the local agent and, in a large part, the Canadian company then began to place it through the head office. In some cases, the actual payment was not made by the Canadian subsidiary corporation to the United States head office corporation. This became a bookkeeping matter as between head office and the local office. The effect was that the Canadian insurers who had been serving these policies no longer receive the Canadian business.
In another, and much more flagrant case, the Canadian subsidiary corporation brought pressure to bear upon its employees in respect of their automobile policies on their privately owned automobiles. All of the employees were requested to cancel out their insurance, and they would receive the same benefits from a master policy which would be
Corporations and Labour Unions held by their Canadian employers. In fact, what happened was that the Canadian subsidiary placed a policy with another general insurance company which was not even licensed to practice within the province of Ontario, and those policies, as placed, cost the individual employees the same amount of money but for less coverage. As a result of the pressure within the company itself, no individual felt that he was in a position to resist. He thought as long as he got the same coverage it would be all right. In fact, all the premiums went to the United States corporation for which the United States head office, and not the Canadian subsidiary, received a very substantial reduction in its over-all fire insurance rates.
These allegations have been presented to me by a responsible officer of the association of fire and casualty agents in this country. If these allegations are correct, they might be the subject of some legislation. I noticed in going through the clauses that the department has not brought forward for the committee any suggestion in respect of insurance privileges. In the first place, I deprecate the phraseology of the motion which I have to put before the committee because I am not a drafter of legislation, but I should like to move at this stage, Mr. Chairman:
That section 4(b) subparagraph (iii) (J) be amended by adding the words "including premiums or payments made for insurance coverage".
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is the only way in which we can ascertain whether or not the allegations which have been made are in fact correct or incorrect. If correct then, as in the case of all other information we obtain from the forms required to be filed under this statute, the committee will be in a position to prepare such legislation as may be required to alleviate the condition.

I was endeavouring to point out to the committee, when I was interrupted, that this is one of those parts of the bill which really has teeth in it. What does it do? It provides that corporations are required to furnish a statement-and this is the first time corporations in the history of Canada will be required to furnish such a statement -showing total amounts paid or credited by the corporation during the reporting period to persons not resident in Canada. This does not appear anywhere else in such specific form.
Let me observe also that with respect to the classes of companies mentioned in the schedule we can get at this information, but the fact remains that this is the first time it has been provided in specific form that corporations should report the amounts paid to persons not resident in Canada, as and on account of each of the following items. I am not going to read the whole list because it is before members of the committee. I think it would be interesting to those who read the report of this debate in Hansard to know in summary what we are going to require. We want to know what corporations pay to people outside of Canada on account of dividends, interest, rents on real property in Canada, rent on equipment used in connection with the business they carry on in Canada, royalties and similar payments including copyrights, patents, industrial designs and trademarks, payments for production, distribution and sales franchises, payments for advertising and sales promotion, and payments in respect of scientific research.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
We want to know what these companies pay to people outside Canada for scientific research. We want to know precisely what the situation is so that we can know what intelligent measures to introduce in order, shall I say, to encourage subsidiary companies in Canada to carry on their scientific research in Canada. We want to know how much they now pay outside Canada for that research.
We also want to know how much they pay to persons outside Canada in respect of product and process development research, how much they pay outside Canada for management and administration fees and charges, how much they pay outside Canada for salaries, fees and other remuneration to officers and directors, how much they pay outside Canada for annuities, pensions and similar payments, how much they pay outside Canada for fees and charges for professional services such as engineering, architectural, legal, accounting and auditing; because it is our view, in accordance with the statement made by the Prime Minister which I have already quoted in this house, that companies carrying on business in Canada, if they are foreign owned, or even if they are subsidiaries of foreign owned companies, should be good Canadians, and that it should be their policy to make these payments in Canada so as to encourage the development of research, management and consultant experience, architectural and engineering skills in Canada instead of paying all these sums to people outside Canada.
But before we can intelligently appreciate what is the situation and know what measures should be taken to bring about desirable changes, if it is necessary for the government to take those measures in order to accomplish that, we want to know what is the present situation and how much is paid outside. Therefore we have provided in this bill that for the first time the government in Canada will have the precise-and I do not hesitate to use that word nor do I apologize for it-the precise information as to what is going on now in these fields.
As I said at the beginning of these remarks, I appreciate what the hon. member for Niagara Falls has done in bringing to our attention that we had overlooked making specific provision that what is paid for insurance to persons outside Canada should also be required to be reported. It could perhaps be argued that it is covered incidentally under some of the other specific things we have provided for, but I do not argue that too strongly. It is acceptable to me, especially in the light of what the hon. member said, that we should make it clear that this heading, which may be a very important heading of

payment to persons outside Canada, should be covered specifically because certainly we have a very excellent, adequate insurance industry in Canada, including life, fire, casualty and other forms. It would certainly be our objective to encourage companies carrying on business in Canada, and profiting by their business in Canada, to place their insurance in Canada with Canadian companies. Therefore as a first step we should know how much they are paying for insurance to companies outside Canada. Accordingly I am prepared to accept the principle of the suggestion that the hon. member has made.
I wonder if the hon. lady would permit me, without being too precise and meticulous, to suggest that the objective could be accomplished better by introducing a separate subheading, rather than by lumping insurance with heading (J), as she tentatively suggested. If it would meet with the approval of the hon. lady I would be prepared to accept an amendment from her which would add, immediately after paragraph (I) of subparagraph (iii), on page 5, a new paragraph (J) which would read "premiums and other charges for or in respect of insurance," and then renumber paragraphs (J) to (N) as paragraphs (K) to (O).

speechtext:
Now that we have begun to discuss another part of this bill, the part in which its provisions are applied to unions, I think we should make some general comments as we did with regard to the provisions affecting corporations. If we assist the minister in the future by remaining silent on one or two clauses I hope he will not accuse us, as he did earlier, completely without justification, of not paying attention.
I may say that we do not consider so-called labour unions, or trade unions, as being foreign controlled or foreign dominated in the same terms as we think of corporations, inasmuch as labour unions are free associations of employees. With respect to a corporation there is usually an importation of capital into the country to establish something in the first place, or to buy up companies in this country or to invest money in them. A trade union or a labour union begins by organizing the members or the employees of a particular

Corporations and Labour Unions company into an organization for their own protection and for the defence of their own interests as differentiated from those of the employer. So I say, as did my hon. friend from Timmins in his opening remarks on the second reading of this measure, that although these two elements in our economy, business corporations and unions, are contained in the same bill there is an essential difference between them. Any attempt to relate one to the other and to suggest they have the same impact upon our economy is not a fair and just comparison. However, they are dealt with in the same bill, and we must consider the matter in that light.
I said in my remarks on the earlier part of this bill that trade unions, as I know them, already file their collective agreements under the various labour acts which exist in the provinces and federally. They file their constitutions. These are public documents, and they enable one to see the true relationship of a local union in Canada to its parent body whether that parent body is in Canada or in the United States. We note that the Department of Labour publishes a monthly labour gazette which gives us a breakdown with regard to collective agreements and their contents. The Department of Labour also publishes annually a document called "Labour Unions in Canada" in which are set out the names of the unions, their officials, the number of locals which exist in Canada and all sorts of other relevant material about them. As I said before, we cannot think about these unions in terms of so-called foreign control; in this respect a comparison with corporations cannot be made. The autonomy of local unions-and this applies generally to all unions I know of-is far greater than the autonomy resting in any Canadian subsidiary of a United States parent corporation. The base of a corporation rests upon the authoritarianism of its managers and is related to seeking profits. The base of a labour union or a trade union-and I differentiate between the two-rests upon the individual members of that union, and these members are the controlling force. I do not know how much weight we can attach to the statement, but the Gordon royal commission recognizes this in its report. It made certain references to unions in the report and said, in effect, the same sort of thing as I have been saying. The commission found no evidence of unions in Canada which did not derive their authority from their membership. There is a vast difference between unions and corporations in this regard.
Thus I think that in this field the information which the government is likely to receive as a result of the requirements of part II of this bill will not help to achieve any object

at all. It will not give the government any understanding of the forces at work in our economy. It will just give them, possibly, information which is not now readily available. One thing it would give, for example, is an indication of the sex of union members. Perhaps that is the sole purpose of the bill. Perhaps some bright person who drafted this bill said: Well, we are going to get all this other useless information so we might as well get the sex of union members, too. I cannot think what value that information will be. It may be thought that female members have more voice, more power in the affairs of unions than male members. I do not know.
I should like to quote some words by one who has been accused of being a member of the labour clique in this nation-one who, apparently, has some domination over this party. I should like to quote some comments by Mr. Bill Mahoney, national director of the United Steelworkers of America. His own words are as follows-there are a number of preliminary remarks, but he goes on to say:
I know of no union which does not give regular and detailed financial statements to its members. Local unions, too, are constitutionally required to present financial reports and undergo periodic audits of their accounts. This can be verified by examination of union constitutions which are filed with the return referred to in paragraph (a) above.
I might as well refer to paragraph (a). It says:
A considerable part of the data specified in section 10 (1) of the bill is already furnished annually to the Department of Labour and most of this is printed in the publication of the economics and research branch of the department, Labour Organization in Canada. The return on which this publication is based includes a list of all local unions with names and addresses of their secretaries. In addition, local unions furnish the names and addresses of their officers and the number of their members on cards circulated by the department.
Because he is the director, he talks about the united steelworkers in particular. I quote again:
The united steelworkers of America, for example, prints twice a year the comprehensive audit report of its independent auditors, Main and Company of Pittsburgh. This report includes statements of income and expenses of the international office and the various district offices, together with a list of fees and dues received from each and every local union. Payments by and expenditures on the two Canadian districts of the union are readily ascertainable from the report. The report also lists the investments in securities and property by the international union.
This report is distributed to every local union in the organization and is printed in our monthly newspaper, Steel Labor, which goes to every member and is available to the public. It is also released to the press. Recently we have been sending it to members of parliament.

This is the essential point:
The availability of financial statements of international unions operating in Canada has been pointed out again and again, in the press and elsewhere. Any demand for legislation on the matter has been part of a synthetic "smear labour" campaign. It is regrettable that the parliament of Canada should be made party to that campaign.
He speaks at length of other aspects of this question, but those are the salient points.
The information sought to be obtained under part II of which clauses 8 and 9 are a part will not contribute anything to the information of the government concerning control of our economy. As in the clause relating to corporations, as I pointed out earlier, the government already receives the information. I do not know why it is required in another form except perhaps to employ more statisticians. This is another indication of the uselessness of this bill.
As far as I can see, the only information the government will receive under this part relates to the sex of union members, how many are male and how many are female. I do not know of what value that would be. Perhaps someone has an interest in this question with a view to publishing statistics showing the number of male and female union members, but I cannot imagine that this would be of value in assessing the effect of foreign interests on our economy. That seems to be the only information that will be obtained under this part. I cannot become too excited in wondering why the minister desires this information.

It has been represented to us therefore that it would be a matter of satisfaction to the trade unions, in furnishing their official returns which here under section A would be open to public inspection and upon which no doubt many annual reports would probably be based, to show the extent of non-discrimination between the sexes in employment in Canada. It does not seem to me that that should give rise to the allegation of discrimination or of some desire to see discrimination on the part of the government which is presenting the bill to the house. All that we are doing is saying that in the return made the number of employees who are male and the number who are female will be stated so that we can see precisely what the position is.
If I were convinced that most of the people in Canada who work or are members of unions felt that this provision somehow or other indicated a desire to discriminate, then I would not attach all that importance to the provision and would be prepared to accept the amendment. However, I doubt that the hon. member has correctly stated the feeling in that regard. I do not think the workers who are members of unions will be greatly concerned because in the return the number of employees who are male and the number who are female have to be shown. I doubt that my hon. friend speaks for the workers of Canada in that regard.
In any event we think it is essential that the numbers of employees should be shown. I could not accept the amendment if only for the reason that it would have the effect of deleting the requirement that the number of employees be stated. I should like to ask the minister a question. In statements he made prior to the introduction of the bill he mentioned the fact that he had examined and given consideration to the United States legislation that applies to labour and management and the fact that it had in it a bill of rights for labour and management which had some effect on the presentation of information. If the government is sincere in wanting to know about some of the difficulties that may arise and certainly have arisen in the United States, this provision could be strengthened considerably and the provisions of the United States legislation might be applied in this instance. It would mean that there would be some guarantee against trusteeships being imposed for reasons not advantageous to the employees in a particular plant, or being imposed in a dictatorial way or for other than legitimate purposes. While the United States bill did a lot more snooping than the government appears to be interested in doing in the bill we have before us, in this instance their bill gave some protection to the employees and union members with relation to trusteeship.
In the main a trusteeship is usually justified for one or two legitimate reasons. It may be that the executive officers of the union have misspent or misused the funds of the local. In other cases the presiding body might put the local under trusteeship for failing to live up to the constitutional requirements as endorsed by the local. Then there are other abuses such as the maintenance of paper locals and so on.
In this instance the minister is asking for the name of each local union or branch of the union in Canada under a trusteeship imposed by the union, the date such trusteeship was imposed and the reasons therefor; and that is all. It would appear to me that the minister is not really interested in correcting the abuse. He wants to find out about it but to me it would seem very inappropriate to find out about the abuse


and then do nothing about It. It may be that if a particular trend develops with regard to abuses in this field the minister may recommend to his colleagues or the dominion statistician may recommend to the cabinet, particularly the Minister of Labour, that there should be an amendment to the bill of rights or under some other statute to provide a remedy for some of the abuses that can take place in this field.
As well as having the name of the local union or branch of the union under trusteeship, the date that the trusteeship was imposed and the reasons therefor, I would think we should also have the names of the people who are the trustees, the amount of the remuneration they are receiving, the constitutional provisions that allow them to impose the trusteeship, the length of time the trusteeship has been in force and other pertinent information which, if it were available, would permit a certain amount of corrective action to be taken, even by the general public.
We have read about the investigations in the United States which have revealed that some unions were not operating in the interests of their membership. It was generally conceded that this was one field in which abuses were most evident and I believe the information asked for in this provision is not sufficient to alert the general public to the full ramifications of what happens under trusteeships, the purpose of trusteeships and what action the local people involved are able to take to reinstate themselves and remove the local from trusteeship or receivership, whichever it happens to be.
I am sure the Minister of Labour could assist in this regard. I suggest there is other information that would bring under public scrutiny some of the abuses that are inherent in the disallowance of constitutions and the imposition of trusteeships on locals by the executive officers of the parent body.
I believe the constitutions themselves are deposited with the Minister of Labour and, in the main, they do cover some of the aspects of trusteeships. If the information were disseminated widely enough, these abuses would be brought to the attention of the general public and allow the general public to have some insight into what was happening in a particular trusteeship. I think this is in keeping with the thought behind the United States reporting bill, that protection can be given to individual employees in a particular plant where trusteeship might be imposed in a manner that was not advantageous to the employees, especially when there might not be an apparent method for getting out of the trusteeship.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I appreciate the concern of the hon. member for Timiskaming with regard to this question of trusteeship and its potential abuses. May I ask him, in turn, to bear in mind that at present the purpose of this bill is to get information concerning what is happening in order to give us the basis upon which we can act to correct abuses. I would suggest to him that the proper place to correct such abuses as there may be in the labour field would be in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, in so far as authority lies within federal jurisdiction. In the same way, the place to correct abuses such as those to which reference was made a little while ago by the hon. member for Skeena in respect of certain activities of corporations, would be in the combines act and not in this bill.
I point out also that, in many respects, the authority to correct malpractices in this field of trusteeship lies in the provincial jurisdiction and not here. If I could get this point across, I should repeat that we have not purported to apply here remedies in this legislation. This measure has as its purpose to give us information on the basis of which remedies may be devised. Certainly, it was not the purpose here to bring in any specific remedy in respect of malpractices under trusteeship. What we wanted to do was to get information as to the circumstances under which trusteeships are imposed, because we understand it is frequently a very direct way of enabling international organizations to exercise direct control over the operations of a union in Canada. We want to find out the extent to which that is being done, and the circumstances under which it is being done. This will cover actually both the provincial and federal fields. When we have the information, then if it is indicated that there are undesirable practices my colleague the Minister of Labour can take action within the sphere of federal jurisdiction and the provincial governments will have the information which will enable them to take action within their sphere of jurisdiction to eliminate these undesirable practices.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I agree that certainly this bill has not gone so far as to take corrective action. The fact that trusteeships have been imposed appears now in a publication of the Minister of Labour, "Canadian Labour Organizations in Canada". This publication indicates how many locals are under trusteeship. Trusteeship is not imposed very often. In my personal experience, I have known several locals to be put under trusteeship. In most cases the reason was the inability of the executive officers to handle the finances of the local. They got themselves into a position
Corporations and Labour Unions where their expenditures were more than their revenues. I think this is a legitimate type of receivership or trusteeship, and is one that is temporary in nature.
However, other locals have, for no particular reason, been put under trusteeship and very little corrective action can be taken by any government, by any authority or even as a result of the knowledge of the public themselves, unless the background circumstances for the trusteeship are given. I think this information should be included in this section. I am aware that the majority of unions use the trusteeship provision in a limited way, and many of them do not use it at all. Those that have used it can usually point to a constitutional clause and I think this information should be included in their return.

They will have to give us those reasons and, in this way, we will be able to amass information as to the kind of circumstances which are being relied upon, the kind of control which is being exercised, and whether it is with justification or without, whether there is a constitutional weakness or just what weaknesses, if any, give rise to an undesirable situation. Is it intended to have one department completely responsible for this information and for publishing statistics in connection with it? Almost every government department has a large conglomeration of information on directorships, ownership of shares and so on-I am thinking particularly of the branch concerned with the supervision of insurance companies. This information is published every year, possibly not in as much detail as we are seeking here. If we were to publish the information we hope to obtain by reason of this bill and make it available for a dollar or two dollars, it might have a certain usefulness and I believe this would be a better way of handling it than the present intention merely to make it available upon payment. If the minister is sincere in his desire to have this information as widely distributed as possible, he might consider this suggestion. We have a library here. I am sure 90 per cent of the people do not go into it, because you can bury anything in those shelves. However, this information could be made available there for scrutiny.
I would strongly recommend that we publish this information on a yearly basis. If there are 25,000 companies affected we might have a fairly heavy document of 500 pages, but it would be available by purchase for those who needed it, if this bill is to serve any purpose at all. Corporations and Labour Unions across the country would be able to use it as background information if it were available in this way. If it is not distributed across the country, a predominance of attention is likely to be paid to it by Ottawa correspondents and other people living in Ottawa such as those connected with the universities in this area; there will not be a national distribution of this information, and I think that if the results are to be effective it should be available on a national basis.

speechtext:
That the said bill be further amended by striking out subsections (3) and (4) of section 14 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
Idem.
"(3) Subsections (1) and (2) do not apply in respect of proceedings relating to the administra-/ tion or enforcement of this act.
Exception re employees of dominion bureau of statistics.
(4)	An official who is an officer or other person employed in the execution of any duty under the Statistics Act or any regulation thereunder may
(a) communicate or allow to be communicated to any other such official any privileged information obtained under this act, and
(b) allow any other such official to inspect or have access to any statement or other writing containing any privileged information obtained under this act.
Exception re other persons for purpose stated.
(5)	Any official or authorized person may, for any purpose relating to the determination of policy in connection with the formulation of any law of Canada or the ascertainment of any matter necessarily incidental thereto,
(a)	communicate or allow to be communicated to any other such person any privileged information obtained under this act, and
(b)	allow any other such person to inspect or have access to any statement or other writing containing any privileged information obtained under this act.
Use of information.
(6)	Notwithstanding anything in this section, in no case shall any privileged information obtained under this act be communicated to any person for the purpose of facilitating the institution or furtherance of any proceedings brought or taken or that may be brought or taken under any law of Canada other than this act."
and by renumbering subsections (5) and (6) of section 14 thereof as subsections (7) and (8), respectively.
Clause 14 stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext: I wonder if I might ask the leader of the house if in indicating the business which the government proposes for tomorrow he could also, as he sometimes does when he is in a benevolent mood, give us a bit of a preview of next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I anticipated that we would have finished this bill today, plus the supplementary estimates, and I was going to call for tomorrow the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister dealing with the electoral boundaries commission. However, we shall have to carry on with the present bill, Bill No. C-38, and complete it tomorrow, followed by supplementary estimates; except that I reserve the right to call, after Bill No. C-38, the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister if, on consultation with him in the morning, it is indicated that he would like to go ahead with it. If that be the case, I will of course advise both parties.
Did I understand the minister to say that will be called as the first item?

speechtext: No; this bill will be the first item, Bill No. C-38.
